“GOD’S EARTH AND MAN’S RESPONSIBILITY” 

by Dr. MacGregor Grant 
Minister, Rosedale United Church , Toronto 


“The earth is the Lord's and the full¬ 
ness thereof; the world, and they that 
dwell therein ” Psalm 24:1. 

Reading through the Bible, we find 
one idea recurring again and again like 
the theme of a symphony: the idea that 
God is the owner of everything and that 
man is merely a trustee, in duty bound 
to carefully administer the earth’s 
resources and to distribute them in 
accordance with the Creator’s wishes. 

Recall such familiar quotations as 
these: “All things come from Thee, C) 
Lord, and of Thine own have we given 
Thee.” Or this: “The silver and the 
gold are Thine; the fruits of the field 
also and the cattle and sheep upon a 
thousand hills.” Or this: “When thou 
hast eaten and art full, then shalt thou 
bless the Lord thy God for the good 
land which He hath given thee.” 

In ancient times, men regarded the 
earth and its fruits with wondering awe. 
As they tilled the soil and garnered their 
crops, they observed mysterious forces 
at work beyond the capability of any 
human agency. Consequently they never 
took the harvest for granted and never 
regarded it as an unaided human 
achievement. Each year, they celebrated 
the Harvest Festival with profound 
reverence, recognizing the fruits of the 
earth as good gifts of God to be grate¬ 
fully received and generously shared. 

The religious significance of Thanks¬ 
giving Day has progressively lessened 
among Canadian city-dwellers and one 
reason for this is that, unlike the Bible 
writers, we do not live close to the soil. 
Consider what even a refrigerator can 


do to dull our sense of dependence on 
God. When people dug up fresh vege¬ 
tables and ate them (perhaps the same 
day) it was easy to remember that 
God’s rain and sunshine made the meal 
possible. But inventions, like refrigera¬ 
tion, have helped to push the Almighty 
out of the picture. Frozen food, gathered 
in California or Texas six months ago. 
tends to make us think of human 
ingenuity rather than the divine bounty. 
Quite unconsciously, we come to assume 
that man is responsible not only for the 
clever electrical appliance but also for 
the fruit and vegetables inside it. It 
takes devastating droughts like those 
experienced last summer in eastern 
Ontario and parts of Quebec to open 
our eyes to the fact that the food in 
our refrigerators would not be there 
apart from factors which are utterly 
beyond human control. 

Today Nature is not something to be 
wondered at and something to be care¬ 
fully preserved, but something to be 
exploited in the name of so-called 
progress. I think it is fair to say that 
the average Toronto citizen is com¬ 
pletely indifferent to the subject of con¬ 
servation of our natural resources. He 
thinks that Canada has an unlimited 
supply of water, timber, orchards and 
fertile farm lands, and that these will 
supply him with all the food he requires 
for centuries to come. He regards those 
who preach the urgent necessity of con¬ 
servation as tiresome alarmists whose 
warnings can be safely disregarded. I 
believe that this attitude is both stupid 
and short-sighted and I am going to 


76 


Canadian Camping 



give you a number of facts which indi¬ 
cate that unless adequate steps are 
taken to preserve our fast-disappearing 
resources, Canada will be involved in a 
disaster of the first magnitude. 

One of our basic resources is water. 
Without a steady supply of pure water, 
life itself could not go on and this 
resource has been dissipated to an 
alarming degree. The situation has 
become so serious in the United States 
that the Americans are proposing to 
import vast quantities of Canadian 
water from the Rocky Mountain 
Trench. After 4 years of continuous 
drought New York City’s reservoirs are 
down to 36% of capacity and still 
falling. 

Things are bad enough in Ontario. 
Our population explosion has changed 
the face of the countryside between 
Oshawa and Hamilton. Housing 
developments, gravel pits, airfields, new 
highways, railway marshalling yards, all 
these have sprung up like mushrooms. 
Nature provided trees and swamps to 
maintain reservoirs of water and when 
these are indiscriminately destroyed, as 
they have been in this area, water 
simply disappears. 

To make matters worse, what water 
we do possess has been seriously con¬ 
taminated. Industries like starch fac¬ 
tories, steel mills and tanneries are 
pouring chemical wastes into our rivers 
and lakes. And municipalities have 
added to the problem by inadequate 
treatment of sewage. Mr. D. B. Waikin- 
shaw of the Metro Conservation 
Authority said recently: “There is not 
a river in Southern Ontario that is not 
polluted.” A fortnight ago, I walked 
beside Duffin’s Creek in the Claremont 
Conservation Park. At Claremont, it is 
a clear, sparkling, lovely stream. But at 
Pickering, where it enters Lake Ontario, 
it is positively filthy. Our once beautiful 
Don River has been turned into a smelly 
ditch and the same thing has happened 
all over Southern Ontario. 


The most disturbing example of our 
criminal negligence is Lake Erie. Thanks 
to the wholesale destruction of timber, 
many of its tributaries have dried up. 
Because of this and because of Ameri¬ 
can industry’s insatiable water require¬ 
ments, the lake level has been lowered 
so that the docks of some cottagers arc 
as much as 200 feet from the nearest 
water. Streams flowing into Lake Erie 
are little more than open sewers and 
sewage and industrial wastes have 
created vast tracts of algae, one of 
which covers an area of 2,500 square 
miles. Since algae deoxygenates water, 
the fish have perished, the Lake Erie 
fishing fleets, once a valuable economic 
asset, have all but disappeared, beaches 
once gleaming with white sand are 
covered with green slime and resort 
areas have had to close down. The 
handwriting is on the wall for all of 
us to read. Unless an aroused public 
opinion forces our timid politicians to 
introduce stringent conservation 
measures, Ontario’s future is dark with 
terrifying possibilities. 

This sermon really sprang out of a 
book I have been reading, Rachel Car¬ 
son’s much discussed “Silent Spring 
It is a hair-raising account of how man 
is destroying Nature by his irresponsible 
use of insecticides. Prior to the Second 
World War, there were less than a 
dozen insecticides in general use. But 
last year, more than 300 varieties were 
on the market and many of them are 
extremely toxic. 

One story told by Miss Carson will 
give you food for sober reflection. In 
1954, the city of East Lansing, in the 
State of Michigan, began to spray its 
trees with D.D.T. in an effort to kill 
the elm bark beetle which is the cause 
of the Dutch elm disease. In addition 
to that, the surrounding countryside 
was sprayed from the air as a control 
measure directed against mosquitoes 
and the gypsy moth. At the same time. 
Professor George Wallace of the Uni¬ 
versity of Michigan (located in East 


Toronto , Canada , April 1966 


77 





Lansing), began a research project to 
discover what the sprays would do to 
the robin population. He asked that 
birds thought to be victims of D.D.T. 
poisoning should be brought to the 
Cranbrook Institute of Science for 
examination. Within a few weeks, over 
a thousand dead robins were turned in. 
And not only robins but 90 different 
species of birds including such well- 
known varieties as sparrows, wrens, nut¬ 
hatches and chickadees. All of these, 
when dissected, were found to have 
D.D.T. in their tissues. 

Now this wholesale slaughter of birds 
which is going on all over the United 
States and Canada is a matter of vital 
concern to each one of us because the 
bird is our most effective weapon in our 
unending war against the insect. Not 
long ago, an Ottawa ornithologist re¬ 
ported dissecting a dead flicker and 
discovering 6,000 insects inside it. And 
what the flicker does all birds do. If the 
bird population is significantly reduced, 
destructive insects will multiply at a 
fantastic rate and our food supply will 
be seriously threatened. This is bound 
to happen if the lethal rain of poisonous 
chemicals goes on increasing as it has 
in the past ten years. 

This is happening in Ontario on an 
ever larger scale. Among farmers, spray¬ 
ing is now standard procedure, for field 
crops as well as orchards. The big 
lumber companies spray their timber 
reserves from the air. Rural municipali¬ 
ties spray the roadsides and the Ontario 
Hydro Corporation sprays its power 
lines. 

In Haliburton last summer, I lived 
in a cottage near a Hydro power line 
and I saw what these sprays can do. A 
team of men came into a lovely stretch 
of woodland and blasted it into a veri¬ 
table wilderness. Tall pines and grace¬ 
ful birches were reduced to black 
skeletons. Over an area extending for 
many miles, every flower, bee, butterfly, 
animal and bird was ruthlessly extermi¬ 
nated. When you consider that this 


sort of thing is happening all over 
Ontario, you realize what it can do to 
our economy. Field crops like potatoes, 
beans, strawberries, indeed any plant 
that bears a flower, must be pollinated 
or it will not bear fruit. But the polli¬ 
nating is done by insects. And every 
pollinating insect destroyed means that 
the productive capacity of Ontario agri¬ 
culture is reduced by just that much. 

Seventy-five years ago, when birds 
like the lark and the robin formed part 
of the diet of the English poor, Ralph 
Hodgson wrote a stinging poem entitled 
“Stupidity Street”. Our chemical war¬ 
fare against the bird, our indispensable 
ally, makes the poem still relevant: 

I saw, with open eyes, singing birds 
sweet 

Sold in the shops for the people to cat, 
Sold in the shops of Stupidity Street. 

I saw, in vision, the worm in the wheat 
And, in the shops, nothing for people 
to eat; 

Nothing for sale in Stupidity Street. 

The Book of Genesis represents God 
as saying to man: “Behold I have given 
you trees to bear fruit and the green 
herb for food. Be fruitful and replenish 
the earth and let the birds of the air 
multiply.” If we continue to disregard 
that commandment, we will suffer for 
it as surely as night follows day. 

What can the individual citizen do to 
preserve our natural resources? One 
thing he can do is read the articles 
on conservation which are constantly 
appearing in magazines and newspapers 
and thus acquire an intelligent under¬ 
standing of this vital problem. I suggest 
that you read Rachel Carson’s “Silent 
Spring ”. You can buy it for a dollar in 
the paperback edition and it wdl open 
your eyes to what is going on. Many of 
you have summer cottages and you can 
exercise constant vigilance in the matter 
of fire prevention. Last week, in Western 
Quebec, a party of picnickers started a 
fire which laid waste 30,000 acres of 
valuable timber. What is the most 
page 87 please 


78 


Canadian Camping 



CAMPING IN CANADA'S NORTH 


SCOUTING IN ARCTIC CANADA 

by B. H. Mortlock 

Secretary, National Arctic and Northern Committee 
on Scouting 
Boy Scouts of Canada 


A visitor to the southernmost tip of 
Canada, around the city of Windsor, 
would hardly be surprised if he were to 
see Boy Scouts hiking along the high¬ 
ways and byways, or to spy their small 
tents nestling in the woods along the 
bank of a sparkling creek, or along the 
shores of a lake. 

He would, however, be very much 
surprised were he to travel 2,000 miles 
north to Grise Fiord on the southern 
shores of Ellesmere Island, 700 miles 
north of the Arctic Circle, and find 
Scouts there too. 

But he would do just that, for at 
Grise Fiord is located Canada’s most 
northerly Scout troop, and possibly the 
most northerly in the world. It is com¬ 
posed of a dozen Eskimo lads under 
the leadership of an RCMP constable 
attached to the police post there. 

And because these Eskimos have 
never seen a tree, or a bicycle, or an 
automobile—which is also true of hun¬ 
dreds of other Eskimo Scouts above the 
tree line—special tests and requirements 
had to be devised to meet their needs 
and to encourage them to retain their 
native crafts and interests. 

Scouting is not new to Canada’s 
Arctic tundra. For more than 25 years 


the Boy Scout program has been avail¬ 
able to Eskimo, Indian and other boys 
living in the north. First taken there by 
missionaries of the Anglican and Roman 
Catholic Churches, it has witnessed 
tremendous expansion during recent 
years, and today there is hardly a com¬ 
munity in the north with more than 
half a dozen boys which has not an 
operating Scout group. 

Leadership is drawn largely from 
white personnel serving in the north as 
missionaries, police officers, Hudson’s 
Bay Company managers and clerks, 
teachers and Northern Service Officers 
of the Department of Northern Affairs, 
and in many cases the wives of such 
personnel. In several communities 
natives are serving as assistant Cub- 
masters and assistant Scoutmasters, and 
the Boy Scouts of Canada anticipates 
the day when all or most of its leader¬ 
ship in the north will be drawn from 
indigenous races. 

Control of Scouting over this huge 
area is vested in the National Arctic 
and Northern Committee of the Boy 
Scouts of Canada, a standing committee 
of the National Council. This com¬ 
mittee is headed by Air Vice-Marshal 
C. H. Green way, commander of North- 


At the Annual Meeting of the Canadian Camping Associa¬ 
tion, held recently in Vancouver, the newest branch — that of 
the North West Territories — was welcomed into membership. 
In order to recognize this significant milestone in our move¬ 
ment’s history, our magazine is publishing a series of articles 
dealing with youth activities related to camping. The first two 
of these appear in this issue. 


Toronto , Canada , April 1966 


79 


ern NORAD, North Bay, Ont. A/V/M 
Greenway succeeded to the chairman¬ 
ship of the committee on the retirement 
of his predecessor, A/V/M J. B. Harvey, 
who organized the original committee 
and headed it until his recent retire¬ 
ment from the RCAF. A/V/M Harvey 
is now Deputy Chief Scout for Canada, 
in which capacity he acts in behalf of 
the Chief Scout, Governor General 
Vanier, in all appropriate matters. 
Other committees in British Columbia, 
Alberta, Manitoba, Quebec and New¬ 
foundland do the actual work of super¬ 
vision in the areas adjacent to them. 

It was under A/V/M Harvey’s 
dynamic leadership over a period of 
several years, and with the full co¬ 
operation of the Northwest Territories 
Council, the Royal Canadian Mounted 
Police, the Department of Northern 
Affairs and others who operate in the 
north, that this expansion was made 
possible. The national committee 
administers an annual grant, made 
available for the promotion and assist¬ 
ance of Scouting in the north by the 
Northwest Territories Council. 

Today there are nearly 2,200 Cubs 
and Scouts in the Mackenzie, Keewatin 
and Franklin Districts of the Northwest 
Territories, in the Yukon, Labrador and 
Arctic Quebec, over which the com¬ 
mittee has oversight. 

In 1968 it is hoped to bring about 
350 of these northern Scouts (mostly 
Eskimo and Indian) to an Arctic Jam¬ 
boree, presently planned to be held in 
Wood Buffalo National Park on the 
Alberta-Mackenzie border. Here at the 
Pine Lake campsite, 40 miles from Fort 
Smith, capital of the Mackenzie, the 
Eskimo Scouts will be joined by 350 
Scouts drawn from every province in 
southern Canada, and for a full week 
boys from north and south will be 
associated together in mixed patrols, 
playing, working, cooking and compet¬ 
ing with each other. The jamboree will 
present a major problem in logistics, 
particularly in the field of transporta¬ 


tion, as many of the Eskimo Scouts live 
in remote communities not served by 
regular commercial airlines. It is hoped 
to bring the boys to central locations in 
the Arctic, from which they will be 
flown by commercial and possibly RCAF 
aircraft to Wood Buffalo Park. The 
boys from southern Canada will likely 
journey to Edmonton by train and fly 
to the campsite from the Alberta capital. 

A strong committee has been organ¬ 
ized, headed by Superintendent Edward 
L. Martin of the RCMP, together with 
officials of the Boy Scouts of Canada 
and representatives of the Northwest 
Territories Council, the Department of 
Northern Affairs, the Indian Affairs 
Branch and commercial airlines serving 
the north. An invitation has been 
extended to American Boy Scouts from 
Alaska to participate. 

The jamboree will not be the first 
time that Eskimo boys have attended 
such an event. Four Eskimo Scouts 
from Resolute Bay attended a jamboree 
in Manitoba two years ago and in 1965 
twenty Eskimo Scouts from Igloolik and 
Frobisher Bay in the Franklin District 
and from Great Whale River in Ungava 
attended the Quebec Provincial Jam¬ 
boree at Drummondville. 

For several years Eskimo Scouts have 
been coming south to camp with their 
brothers in other provinces, and Mont¬ 
real’s Gamp Tamaracouta has conduct¬ 
ed a program of such visits for a number 
of years. Jonah Kelly, an Eskimo Scout 
from Frobisher Bay, has three times 
joined an Ottawa troop at summer 
camp, which included camping trips to 
Atlantic City and Philadelphia. 

Two Scouts from Edmonton paid a 
week-long visit to Resolute Bay on 
Cornwallis Island, where they learned 
what life was like in the farthest reaches 
of Canada’s northland. 

Many regular Scout tests and badges 
are not suitable for Arctic Scouts because 
of the terrain in which they live, so 
specially adapted tests have been 
developed and a whole scries of special 


80 


Canadian Camping 



proficiency badges devised. These were 
the work of men long associated with 
the north and are intended primarily 
to encourage Eskimo boys to retain the 
crafts for which their culture is noted. 

Available to Arctic Scouts now arc 
badges for hunting, skinning, igloo 
building, carving, lamp making, fur 
trapping, dog driving and several others. 
In many cases these badges were 
designed by Eskimo Scouts themselves 
in a competition planned by the Arctic 
and Northern Committee. 

Weather conditions in the north, 
cold, black flies and mosquitoes, do not 
permit the full Scout uniform being- 
worn, but the boys proudly wear the 
Scout shirt and hat, and in Resolute 
Bay the Scouts designed their own hats. 

Made possible by the grant from the 
Northwest Territories Council, special 
training courses arc held for Scout 
leaders serving in the north, and such 
courses have been held in Inuvik, 


Yellowknife and Frobisher Bay. These 
Arctic training courses would be impos¬ 
sible to achieve were it not for the 
generosity of several airlines serving the 
Arctic which have made space available 
for trainers and trainees alike on their 
aircraft. Missionaries in the north have 
provided accommodation for the courses. 
Some leaders take training during the 
summer months when they come south 
for vacations. 

It is of interest to note that the sister 
movement, the Girl Guides of Canada, 
arc as actively engaged in youth work 
as the Boy Scouts and serve as many 
or perhaps more than the Boy Scout 
Movement. 

As new communities grow around 
new mining and oil developments in 
the Arctic, Scout groups are formed, 
and it is anticipated that Scouting 
throughout the Arctic will continue 
steadily to grow in the years ahead. 


PRAYER OF ST. FRANCIS (1182-1226) 

Lord make me an instrument of Thy peace: 

Where there is hatred, let me sow love: 

Where there is injury, pardon; 

Where there is discord, harmony; 

Where there is error, truth; 

Where there is doubt, faith; 

Where there is despair, hope; 

Where there is darkness, light; 

Where there is sadness, joy. 

O Divine Master, grant that I may not so much seek 
To be consoled as to console, 

To be understood as to understand, 

To be loved as to love; 

For it is in giving that we receive; 

It is in self-forgetting that we find; 

It is in pardoning that we are pardoned; 

It is in dying that we are born to eternal life. 


Toronto , Canada , April 1966

CAMl* REUNIONS 



A trip to camp is all we need at this depressing time-o 
To make us pack our duffel bags and head for warmer clime-o. 

The roofs all sag, the floors look warped, the windows rife with cracks. 

The woods are stuffed to bursting with forgotten boots and macks. 

Tent platforms have alarming lists to one side or the other 
The boathouse roof is just the thing our insurance does not cover! 

The ancient sailboats have to go: they’re always simply soaking. 

Fhe tennis courts have horrid holes where groundhogs have been poking. 

The Nature Trail has caven in: the bridge of course is rotten. 

Where is the seasoned wood, alas! which we had thought we’d boughten? 

The applications stopped last week, for no apparent reason. 

It’s obvious, at once, that WE’LL RE IN FHE RED THIS SEASON! 

Our Senior Staff’s to Europe off. just when we really need them. 

And prayers, entreaties, e’en our DOUGH, they simply scorn to heed them. 

O! Why then do we hesitate; why don’t we find a buyer? 

And just retire to Mexico, with climate so much dryer? 

Why don’t we leave the ills behind, that all Camp I firs, are heir to. 

And spend our time in slothful ease, sunbathing when we care to? 

Because, one snowy Saturday, regardless of the weather 
We made a plan (we must be MAD!), to get the gang together. 

We sang old songs, revived old jokes, and brought the summer nearer. 

What we’d but dimly understood was suddenly made clearer. 

What mattered it if boats DID leak, and docks heaved in the middle? 

What mattered it if roofs DID sag. caused by the termite’s riddle? 

What mattered most was kids themselves, with all their maddening habits. 
Let’s run our camps with insight. TO PREVENT THEIR BEING BABBITS! ! 

—Joyce Bertram, 

Camp Ouareau, P.Q.

CAMPING FIRE SAFETY 


Have you ever gazed into a camp 
fire and wondered what fire is and 
what makes it burn? If you know the 
answer to these questions you will have 
a better understanding of how to con¬ 
trol or prevent a fire. 

For fire to occur, three elements 
must be present—fuel, heat and oxygen. 
As air contains a sufficient proportion 
of oxygen for fire to occur, it is simpler 
to refer to the elements as fuel, heat 
and air. In conjunction these are called 
the Triangle of Fire. 


Heat 

By studying the Triangle of Fire a 
knowledge of fire extinguishment can 
be attained. It is simply the removal 
of one or more of the three elements. 
An illustration of this is a gas stove fire 
which can be extinguished by simply 
closing off the fuel supply. 

This principle of extinguishment is 
very easy to put into efiect on a fire 
in its incipient stage. In a major fire 
the same principle applies but due to 
many other factors, extinguishing the 
fire calls for specialized techniques and 
equipment. However, we are not con¬ 
cerned with extinguishing large fires, 
this is a job only for trained fire 
fighters. We are concerned with ex¬ 
tinguishing small fires in their incipient 


stage particularly in camping areas 
where the supply of fire extinguishers 
is generally limited. 

Fires are classified as to the fuel 
burning and by applying the principle 
of removing one of the elements of the 
Triangle of Fire, the fire can be 
quickly extinguished. 

Class “A” fires arc fires involving 
ordinary materials such as paper, can¬ 
vas, wood, dry grass and vegetation. 

In tiiis type of fire it is usually im¬ 
possible to remove the fuel. The air 
could possibly be removed by blanket¬ 
ing it ofl, but then this type of fire is 
usually deep seated and blanketing or 
smothering would be of little use. The 
only remaining element possible to re¬ 
move is heat and this can be accomp¬ 
lished by the cooling application of 
water. 

Class “B” fires are fires involving flam¬ 
mable liquids, fats and greases. The 
action of the cooling agent such as 
water usually tends to spread the fire 
as the burning fuel floats on top. The 
removal of the fuel is not too practical 
except in the case of a gas stove fire 
as mentioned previously. The most 
efficient method of extinguishing this 
class of fire is by the removal of air or 
smothering. 

Class “C” fires are those involving 
electrical equipment. In this type of 
fire there is the danger of electric shock. 
This hazard can be eliminated by using 
an extinguishing agent that is non- 
conductive. The fuel can be removed 
by shutting ofl' the power or the fire 
can be extinguished by smothering. 

In most camping areas the perm¬ 
anent buildings are usually well equip¬ 
ped with fire extinguishers. These 
extinguishers are for the protection of 
camp buildings and are usually too far 




Toronto , Canada , April 1955 


83 



removed from the camp area to be of 
use in an emergency. 

In camping areas the most common 
type of extinguishers available is the 
back pack or knapsack extinguisher. 
This type of extinguisher usually con¬ 
tains two to four gallons of water and 
is operated by a hand action pump. 
Campers should read the operating in¬ 
structions on the water container in 
order to familiarize themselves with its 
operation. 

Many campers today cany small 
dry chemical extinguishers in their ve¬ 
hicles or trailers. These arc usually 
the 2/z to 5 lb. size and can be trans¬ 
ferred from car to boat and back to 
camp with no difficulty. This type of 
extinguisher is excellent for use on Class 
“B” to “C” fires and can also extinguish 
small Class “A” fires if they arc not 
deep seated. 

Most experienced campers know 
that they must rely on their own re¬ 
sources in the event of a fire, particu¬ 
larly in its incipient stage. Should a 
fire occur which cannot be quickly 
extinguished with available equipment 
—send for help immediately and warn 
persons nearby. Then do your best to 
contain and control the fire until assist¬ 
ance arrives; but only without endan¬ 
gering your life. 

Many small fires can be quickly ex¬ 
tinguished by improvising and using 
ordinary camping equipment. A broom 
is an ideal tool to use in beating out a 
small grass fire in a camp area. A 
blanket can be used to smother a fire. 
This is a particularly efficient method 
if the banket can be wet down with 
water before using. 

Sand and earth are excellent smoth¬ 
ering agents when shovelled into a fire. 
If a shovel is not available use the lid 
ofF a pot or pan. 

Bicarbonate of soda or salt can be 
sprinkled on a small grease fire but be 


careful that you do not splash the 
grease on your clothing or skin. 

A full thermos of drinking water or 
a bucket of dish water can effectively 
extinguish a surprisingly large fire if 
used with discrimination. 

One of the cardinal rules in camping 
is to maintain a clean campsite. This 
in itself can eliminate many possible 
sources of fire. 

Empty bottles can start a fire by 
magnifying the sun’s rays. For this 
reason they should always be wrapped 
up and disposed of with the camp 
garbage. 

Rubbish, dried vegetation, twigs and 
branches should be cleaned up and 
disposed of as they cause the rapid 
spread of fire. 

Camp fires should never be lit with¬ 
out a permit from the park or camping 
area authorities, and then only in the 
area specified. Never leave a camp fire 
unattended, always extinguish it with 
water and stir and mix the ashes to 
ensure that it is completely out. 

Beware of the wind if you light a 
camp fire in an open area. If the wind 
rises, extinguish the fire and move to 
a sheltered area. 

Always remember that “earth” on 
the surface in forested areas is mostly 
powdered dead leaves, and will burn 
and smoulder for hours. 

Avoid smoking while walking or 
hiking in the woods. Smoke during 
rest periods and extinguish your pipe 
embers or cigarettes in water or on 
a flat rock. 

Our parks and forests are part of 
our heritage and have been preserved 
in their natural state for our enjoyment 
and appreciation. A little thought and 
care today will protect and preserve 
this heritage for future generations. 

Department of Public Works, 
Fire Prevention Branch, 
Ottawa

How Do you Score On fire Safety ? 

Score your camp’s fire safety. Next to each question are two boxes to be 
answered by a check mark in cither YES or NO. Each question answered NO 
points to a serious fire hazard. Do something about these hazards—now! Use 
tile check list at the opening of camp. Consult it frequently during the season. 
Save your camp — save your forest from fire. 


HOUSEKEEPING 

1. Have you removed all flammable rubbish and leaves from around buildings 

and tents? . 

2. Are grass, bush and small trees cut or thinned out around camp buildings? 

3. Is fire-fighting equipment within easy reach when trash, leaves, etc., are 

burned out-of-doors? . 

4. Do you keep your storerooms and garages free from rubbish, old rags, 

papers, etc.? . 

5. Do you keep oil mops or paint rags in closed metal containers to guard 

against spontaneous ignition? . 

6. Are stoves always kept free of grease? Do you have baking soda or salt 

handy in case of grease fires? . 

7. Do you hang towels on special racks, never drying them on or near stoves? 

8. Do you collect ashes in covered hole-free metal containers and dispose of 

them when properly cooled? . 

9. Do you keep matches in metal containers away from heat? . 

10. Do you use only safety matches in camp? . 

11. Do you have spark-screens over all chimneys? . 

12. Are all fireplaces equipped with effective fire-screens? . 

FLAMMABLE LIQUIDS 

13. Do you start fires with paper and/or kindling only, never with flammable 

liquids? . 

14. Arc kerosene or gasoline lanterns hung up or put on tables or shelves and 

never on the floor? . 

15. Are supplies or fuel oil stored away from buildings', in underground tanks? 

16. Arc oils (kerosene and gasoline) handled only in the daylight and where 

spillage cannot be ignited? . 

17. Are gasoline stoves and kerosene stoves and heaters of types listed by 

Underwriters’ Laboratories, Inc.? . 

18. Are your lamps sufficiently heavy-based to prevent tipping? . 

CONSTRUCTION 

19. Are the roofs of your buildings non-combustible? . 

20. Arc roofs, gutters, caves of buildings free of needles and leaves? . 

21. Are all stovepipes, chimneys and hoods above kitchen stoves cleaned and 

repaired before camp opens? . 

22. Arc floors directly under stoves* and heaters protected by galvanized iron, 

concrete or brickwork? . 

23. Have you eliminated all stovepipes which pass through closets or storerooms? 

24. Arc walls, rafters, ceilings and partitions protected from over-heating of 

stoves and pipes? . 


CHECK

No

WHERE IS IT ? 

by Josephine Harshaw 
Editor, “Canadian Camping” 

I think we’cl all agree that we would 
feel much more confident exploring 
new trails or tramping over unfamiliar 
terrain, if we have a compass in our 
pocket. 

Even that widely travelled and 
intrepid explorer, Samuel de Cham¬ 
plain, carried a compass on his numer¬ 
ous treks. Only in those days it was 
called an “astrolabe”. Originally de¬ 
signed by the Babylonians, it was quite 
an ancient instrument by Champlain’s 
time and in fact its manufacture was 
discontinued about 161 i. 

We wish we could include an illustra¬ 
tion of an astrolabe but, if you want to 
see an actual photograph of Cham¬ 
plain’s, perhaps your local library can 
help you. Ask if they have a copy of 
Canon Henry Scadding’s “Astrolabes of 
Samuel de Champlain and GeofTrey 
Chaucer”, published 1880, “On Cham¬ 
plain’s Astrolabe” by A. J. Russell. 
1879, or P. J. Robinson’s “Toronto 
During the French Regime”, published 
1934/ 

Meanwhile we can tell you that 
Champlain’s astrolabe was a thick, 
brass, circular disc, finely marked off 
towards the outer edge in 360 degrees. 
It was 5%" in diameter and weighed 
about three pounds. There were four 
petal-shaped openings and a moveable 
bar which pivoted at the centre. It 
could be suspended by using a heavy- 
looking ring attached to a thick stem 
at the top or be held in the hands. 

Astrolabes were particularly useful in 
taking the altitude of stars and other 
heavenly bodies. Consequently they 
were of real help in determining lati¬ 
tudes and so were much used by navi¬ 
gators. It is not surprising then that 


Champlain carried one on his Canadian 
journeyings. 

In late May and early June of 1613. 
Champlain, four other Frenchmen and 
an Indian guide were exploring the 
country adjacent to what is now Ren¬ 
frew county. In describing this journey, 
and especially the portage between Lake 
Allumette and Muskrat Lake, Cham¬ 
plain says they were all greatly over¬ 
burdened; he undertook to carry some 
of the various goods and chattels, “biens 
et diets”. Added to this they were con¬ 
stantly harassed by hordes of mosquitoes 
which swarmed over them, causing them 
great physical discomfort and impeding 
their progress. 



Under such circumstances it is quite 
understandable that even such essential 
equipment as an astrolabe could fall out 
of a 1613 version of a kit bag and its 
loss go unnoticed until a day or two 
later. Perhaps Champlain discovered 
his loss when he and his companions 
reached the site of what later became 
the town of Pembroke. Apparently he 
tried to estimate the latitude but a 
marked error in his calculations led to 
the belief that this was due to his then 
being without his astrolabe. 

More than two and a half centuries 
later, in the year 1867, a farmer named 
Overman, ploughing virgin soil on the 
banks of the Ottawa River in the town¬ 
ship of Ross, near Renfrew, turned up 
a brass disc blackened with age but 
wonderfully preserved. It bore the date 
1603 and almost certainly was the one 
lost by Champlain. 

Later it came into the possession of 
another navigator, Captain Overman, 
probably a relative of the farmer, who 


86 


Canadian Camping 



presented it to the President of the 
Ottawa Forwarding Company. Richard 
S. Cassells. In 1875 Mr. Cassells became 
a resident of Toronto and after his 
death his son, Walter Gibson Cassells, 
sold the astrolabe on September 10, 
1901, to an American collector, Samuel 
V. Hodman of Paul Smiths, N.Y. 

One other astrolabe turned up on 
Christian Island in the Georgian Bay. 
Dated 1595, it was found in 1925 and 
is supposed to have been used by Jesuit 
missionaries in making early maps. 

The Toronto Daily Star of Novem¬ 
ber 28, 1927, carried an article under 
the provocative title, “Where is Cham¬ 
plain’s Astrolabe?”. Not having seen 
the article, we do not know what 
answer was given—or if the question 
remained unanswered. 

Would any Camp Directors or their 
campers like to find out where Cham¬ 
plain’s astrolabe is now and let us 
know? 


God's Earth 
from page 7$ 

destructive animal on the face of the 
earth? Not the tiger, not the wolf, but 
MAN, whose criminal folly has so dis¬ 
sipated his God-given assets. 

I have entitled this sermon “God’s 
Earth and Man’s Responsibility” and 
as I bring my remarks to a close 1 want 
to stress the fact that conservation is 
more than an economic necessity. It is 
a religious duty as binding as the Ten 
Commandments. In the sanctuary today 
we are surrounded by the fruits of the 
earth, impressive symbols of the divine 
goodness and v isible reminders of the 
fact that we are stewards and trustees 
of a precious heritage. So. let us make 
sure that our thanksgiving is not just 
empty words but a prelude to act : on. 
Let us resolve that we will do our part 
to preserve the good land which God has 
given us and to transmit it unharmed 
and unimpaired to generations yet 
unborn.

CRAFTS AT SERPENT RIVER 

by Eileen Muff 

Crafts Adviser on staff of Community Programs Division 
Ontario Department of Education 


Ever since a time several years age 
when I spent four days with the people 
of the Couchiching Reserve near Fort 
Frances, I have wanted to learn as 
much as I could about the native handi¬ 
crafts of our Indians. These people 
seemed to be natural craftsmen and had 
convinced me that, with the right kind 
of help, their hands could easily rc-lcarn 
the old crafts that were so important in 
the lives of their ancestors. 

I discussed these ideas with Jane 
Bartlett, a social worker attached to the 
Indian Affairs Branch. She told me 
that the old techniques were disappear¬ 
ing so quickly that it was difficult to 
find anyone willing and able to teach 
them. However, she knew of a Mrs. 
Mcawasigc who lived at Serpent River 
near Blind River, an excellent basket 
weaver. She promised to let me know 
if anything could be arranged. 

Some months later I heard from Miss 
Bartlett that a course in basket-weaving 
was being planned at Serpent River. In 
a great state of excitement I left 
Toronto one April Sunday evening and 
stepped off the “Soo Line” train the 
next morning at Cutler. I was still five 
or six miles from Serpent River but a 
car was there to meet me and we drov e 
to the home of Mrs. Shawana for lunch. 

After lunch I was a little startled to 
learn that the material for the baskets 
was not prepared. In fact the black ash 
from which our baskets were to be 
made was still standing in the bush 
somewhere, and the plan was that we 
should now set out to find it. Somehow 
this first step had never occurred to me. 


Later I realized that I should never 
have really understood the craft if they 
had not been wise enough to arrange 
this trip for me. It would certainly have 
been easier for them to have gone to 
the bush for the ash the week before, 
and to have had the strips all prepared. 

We set of! for Sucker Creek with our 
guide Jim Jacobs, who lapsed into his 
native Ojibway as soon as we started 
into the bush. He had told me that 
English was good enough for everyday, 
and French was best for profanity, but 
only an Indian language was suitable 
for the bush. And indeed the soft 
syllables and musical cadences seemed 
part of that carly-spring setting. He 
did not speak English again until we 
returned to the village, but the ladies 
translated his instructions and his jokes 
for me. 

Even in this country the black ash 
has become scarce. We found two or 
three trees that had to be rejected 
because their trunks were not straight. 
When we found the tall, erect tree that 
suited our purpose, Mr. Jacobs instruct¬ 
ed the women to make the cooking-fire 
while he felled the tree. 

The fire was quickly made and then 
the ladies produced from their knap¬ 
sacks pats of bannock dough, each 
carefully wrapped in wax-paper, large 
skillets, bacon, tea and butter. Each 
package of dough was flattened to fit 
into a heated skillet and cooked in a 
few minutes over the hot fire. The 
bacon was toasted on improvised twig 
forks, and the tea water boiled in a 
can suspended over the fire. We split 


88 


Canadian Camping 



and buttered the hot bannock, sand¬ 
wiching our bacon between the layers. 
I never enjoyed a more fortifying and 
delicious afternoon tea. 

During the trip I had not distin¬ 
guished myself for woodsmanship, but 
everyone had been very good-natured 
and kind about my stumbling, awkward 
city ways. Now, however, it was dis¬ 
covered that I had even been stupid 
enough to come without a drinking cup 
for my tea. One of the women padded 
off and came back in a few minutes 
with a neat rectangle of birch-bark 
which she quickly folded and fastened 
into a perfectly water-tight cup for me. 

While lunch was being prepared, Mr. 
Jacobs had cut a four-foot ash log for 
us, and he had removed the bark along 
a four-inch strip. With his help we were 
to pound over this barked area with 
the backs of our axes until the strip of 
white wood began to spring away from 
the dark heart of the log. As the strip 
separated a wedge was put in and the 
pounding continued down the length of 
the log. When the whole strip was 
free, the pounding began on the next 
one. 

Once again my shortcomings were 
glaringly apparent. I could barely lift 
the axe, let alone raise it over my head 
and bring it down with a thump calcu¬ 
lated to separate that springy strip from 
the log. The other women each took a 
turn, along with Mr. Jacobs, and by 
late afternoon we had enough ash 
stripped. We started back toward the 
village with our bundles of ash. One of 
Mr. Jacob’s last remarks in Ojibway 
before we left the bush caused a great 
deal of mirth amongst the ladies. They 
hesitated to translate it for me but I 
insisted. “White woman no good, leave 
her in the bush”, was the best they 
could do for me in English. 

The next day we all gathered in 
the community hall where we cleaned, 
scraped and dyed the strips of ash. We 
were shown how to separate the layers 


and to scrape each side with a knife 
so that it was quite smooth. The final 
splitting revealed two creamy, satin- 
smooth surfaces. These strips were then 
cut into the desired widths and rolled 
into skeins ready for the yellow, orange 
and brown dye-baths. 

When our ash strips were dry once 
more, we began to weave our baskets, 
and in the following days the group 
produced a dozen or so baskets in many 
sizes, shapes and colour combinations. 
We all enjoyed working together and 
our conversation finally led to the idea 
of forming a group that would meet 
regularly to learn crafts of different 
kinds. I promised to return before long 
and to teach them how to weave textiles. 

Before I left for the city, the new 
group had even chosen a dignified and 
suitable name for itself — the Chitamo 
Graft Club of the Serpent River Reserve. 
“Chitamo” is the Ojibway name for the 
busy, chattering squirrels of the north 
woods. It was also the Indian name of 
our instructor, Agnes Meawasige. 

In the fall I returned to Serpent 
River to keep my promise. Miss Bartlett 
had helped the group to make the 
advance arrangements for the three-day 
course in box-loom weaving. Yarns and 
other supplies were on hand, and small 
box-looms had been built according to 
a plan and specifications I had sent 
along during the summer. They had 
also invited two ladies from Garden 
River, and two others from Mikwemi- 
kong on Manitoulin Island, to join the 
class. 

The first day of any weaving course 
for beginners is usually long and diffi¬ 
cult. There arc so many small details 
to master before any sign of progress 
can be seen. Most new students find it 
hard to realize how firmly the weaver 
must grip the warp to make it even: 
they are usually tentative and clumsy. 
Instinctively these women grasped their 
materials with the hands of craftsmen 
and carried out ail the instructions 


Toronto, Canada, April 1966 


89 



with hardly a wasted movement. The 
younger women, who learned very 
quickly, did not need to be asked to 
stop and help the older, slower learners 
through each step so that the whole 
class could move along at about the 
same rate. In record time they were 
all weaving interesting designs develop¬ 
ed from their own fascinating choices 
of colour combinations. Their interest 
was as keen on the third day as it had 
been on the first. 

This was one of the shortest weaving 
courses I ever conducted, but the results 
in the intervening three years have been 
encouraging. The group has continued 


to meet and they have accepted the 
responsibility of teaching other Indian 
groups to weav e. Mrs. Agnes Mcawasige 
has inspired and taught several classes; 
a recent one was at Naughton where 
the students worked out all the details 
of the organization and content for 
themselves. 

I remain convinced that this ex¬ 
change, in which I received more than 
I gave, represents a pattern that might 
be used in many places to revive the 
interest of Indian groups in useful crafts 
generally, and in their own native crafts 
in particular. 



to share with your counterparts across 
the country some of the things that are 
said or done at your camp? 

Well, “Canadian Camping” is going 
to give you an opportunity to do just 
that. Camping days will soon be here 
again. And when they are and when 
your camp is in full swing and when 
you’re observing what goes on or over¬ 
hearing what is said in those less self- 
conscious moments, please remember 
“Canadian Camping” and the column 
being initiated with this issue. 

We’re calling it “From a Camp 
Director’s Diary” and we hope you’ll 
share those amusing, unusual or just 
plain interesting incidents or comments 
that are a part of every camp. 

Jot it down, send it in and we’ll do 
the rest.

The whole camp was in a great state 
of excitement as wc mentioned the pos¬ 
sibility of entering a float in the Hali- 
burton “Monster Parade” as the Rotary 
Club called it in their poster which 
circulated the countryside. Size of the

she said quite seriously: “But won’t our 
camp look terribly silly with campers 
in the parade when everybody else has 
Monsters?”.

HOOTENANIES 


Now-a-days hootenannies are part of 
every camp program. Plunking, strum¬ 
ming, singing goes on at all hours of 
the clay (and of the night, too, on 
occasion). The campers, counsellors, 
and staff who bring their instruments 
to camp love to get together to ex¬ 
change songs, learn new chords, or a 
different method of strumming their 
? ukes’, banjos or guitars. 

It is a little difficult for camp direc¬ 
tors, who belong to another generation, 
to be knowledgeable about these in¬ 
struments. Usually a dealer will give 
good advice, but what they need is 
specific information. 

Here it is. There are four types of 
ukuleles, standard size, tenor, baritone, 
and dixie banjo. Banjos have either 
four or five strings. Guitars have be¬ 
come very popular. The nylon stringed 
classic guitar is favoured by most 
amateur folk singers. Cheaper guitars 
do not have much tone but can be 
replaced more economically. A proper 
bag or case should be purchased for an 
instrument to protect it from damp¬ 
ness, dryness or accident. 

Bongos, claves, castanets, maraccas, 
and Congo drums are fun to play and 
will add to a sing-song or a hoote¬ 
nanny. Other rhythm instruments can 
be purchased cheaply, tambourines, 
woodblocks, sand blocks, rhythm sticks, 
etc. Stores which sell rhythm band 
instruments are your best bet for these. 

What about a kazoo band? There 
is also a hum-a-zoo. A piece of paper 
over a comb will give the same effect. 

Some pre-band instruments which 
are easy to learn to play are song 
flutes, tonettes, and flutophones. Then 
there is an instrument which is fun 
for everybody to learn to play, a 


by Mary Paton , 

St, Christopher House, Toronto 


Melodica by Hohner; it sounds some¬ 
thing like a harmonica. The keyboard 
is like a piano with black and white 
keys; extra mouthpieces give oppor¬ 
tunities for a number of campers to use 
the same instrument. (And don’t for¬ 
get harmonicas.) 

Autoharps are being used by folk 
singers too. They resemble zithers but 
have an arrangement of bars. The 
instrument is either plucked or 
strummed and as each bar is pushed 
down a different chord is heard. 

A piano at camp can be a great 
help. Keep it well-tuned and in good 
repair and it will last for a long time. 
An excellent pianist makes a great 
difference to a sing-song; and is also 
available for concerts, folk dancing, 
operettas and countless other things. 

For a chapel service in the woods 
where there is no pump organ, a 
guitar, accordion, or autoharp can be 
used to provide music for the hymns. 

Having instruments available for 
campers to experiment with, pays off. 
Even the piano will be used by the 
camper to sit and pick out a tune on 
it. So can almost all the other instru¬ 
ments; whatever you think a camper 
will enjoy. There are instructions on 
how to play some of them, and these 
can be left with the instruments; those 
who want them will study them, but 
some will just want to experiment. If 
there is a request for more formal 
instruction, this can easily be arranged. 
Before instruments are left out, some 
explanation of how to use and look 
after them should be made to campers 
and counsellors alike. A melodica must 
be blown out after use, and the reason 
should be given; a demonstration is in 

♦ 


Toronto, Canada, April 1966 


91 



order. Wooden instruments should be 
put in eases. The counsellors will make 
as much use of the instruments in free 
time as will campers. 

Arts and crafts books give informa¬ 
tion on making musical instruments 
which can be used at camp. 

The cost of instruments varies 
greatly. Instruments which a great 
number of campers will use, must be 
-able to stand up. Some instruments can 
stand rougher treatment than others, 
but the proper care of all instruments 
is essential if they arc to last.

“MY FEET...” 

If you can solemnly swear you’ve 
never, ever exclaimed, “My feet are 
killing me”, you don’t need to read 
this. But, if you can’t and you’re a 
person who likes to walk or go on a 
hike, especially when spring beckons: 
if you’re yearning for camping days or 
holiday time so that you can “hit the 
trail” again perhaps you’d better keep 
on reading. And, as your feet are going 
to be your means of transportation, it 
might be well to ponder how you can 
ensure that they will sene you well. 
Here, then, are some hints on foot care 
which we’ve just come across. 

If your feet have been giving you any 
persistent discomfort, you should get 
medical advice. If not, you can con¬ 
centrate on some conditioning that will 
strengthen your foot and ankle muscles 
and toughen the skin. 

Exercising your feet can be done in 
odd moments and, as this generally 
involves the toes, slip off your shoes and 
relax. A good basic exercise is picking 
up a pencil with the toes; try it 20 
times with each foot. Another one— 
sit in a chair, legs straight out; squeeze 
toes under tightly and bend ankles so 
that feet point toward body as far as 
possible. Then bend feet away from 
body, still keeping toes curled tightly. 
Repeat ten times. 

While standing, twist feet so that 
heels are turned out, toes in; press toes 
down as hard as possible. This arch- 
strengthening exercise is helpful; stand 
with toes extended over the edge of a 
thick book or step and bend toes down 
as far as possible. Practise walking with 
toes straight ahead and make them grip 
the floor with each pace. Rise slowly 
on tiptoes, thrusting weight on to toes. 

Skin toughening is a precaution 
against blisters. Frequent massages with 


92 


Canadian Camping 

























rubbing alcohol or salt or epsom salts 
bathing will help feet resist the abrasive 
action of long distance walking. 

And when you’re actually on the hike 
there are some things you can do for 
your feet, too. Frequent short rests arc 
more beneficial than fewer long stops. 
Relax with the feet propped higher 
than the body. If possible bathe your 
feet in a cool, clear stream (beware of 
polluted water) or massage with alcohol 
and apply any good foot powder. Ease 
of! the boot laces during a halt and at 
mid-day change to a fresh pair of socks. 
Or air out the socks you have been 
wearing, turn them inside out and 
switch them to opposite feet. 

Any “hot” or sensitive skin areas 
should be treated with antiseptic oint¬ 
ment and protected from further chaff¬ 
ing with adhesive tape or gauze band¬ 
age. Blisters should not be given any 
“do it yourself’ treatment. Take every 
precaution to avoid having them but if 
a blister develops do consult the camp 
doctor immediately. This will eliminate 
the likelihood of any distressing and 
inconvenient infection. 

Be sure that your footwear — socks 
and shoes—are in good condition and 
adequate for the conditions likely to be 
met on the trail. The sock combination 
found most effective by outdoorsmen is 
a good-quality fine knit wool and cotton 
sock fitting snugly next to the skin; over 
this goes a good quality all-wool sock, 
coarse knit to provide a cushion. The 
theory is that cotton will absorb per¬ 
spiration and resilient wool will create 
a pumping action for air circulation. 

Sensible demands from your feet will 
make them “last longer and finish 
stronger”. Toughen up gradually. Take 
it easy in the beginning days of walking 
or hiking or hitting the trail. But don’t 
loaf all the way. By forcing yourself to 
the limit in easy stages, your speed and 
endurance will improve and your enjoy¬ 
ment will increase. 

So good hiking in 1966.

SASKATCHEWAN’S ADVENTURE 

IN 

INTERNATIONAL CAMPING 1965 


by Doris M. Grassie 

Chairman sub-committee for Guest Camper Program , Saskatchewan 
Diamond Jubilee and Centennial 

Children and Teen Program and Camp Director, YWCA, Regina 


The idea of intcr-cultural camping 
was born of a natural curiosity about 
people—plus a heritage from pioneer 
stock, having lived in several Ethnic- 
centred communities, as well as contact 
in the YWCA with all races, cultures 
and creeds and the following experience 
in a club group. As a result of a chance 
remark, a group of children hailing 
from a variety of Ethnic origins dug 
into the memories of parents and rela¬ 
tives for stories of their homeland and 
brought treasures to show and discuss 

The camp opportunity came through 
membership in the Saskatchewan 
Diamond Jubilee and Centennial sub¬ 
committee for Youth Steering. Each 
member was requested to list projects 
for the Centennial year. Youth Camps 
appeared on several lists and on think¬ 
ing about Saskatchewan and the many 
countries combined in the mosaic of its 
population, an inter-cultural exchange 
appeared appropriate. 

I found myself chairman of a won¬ 
derful committee, with instructions to 
prepare a brief for the Corporation, 
outlining a plan of operation. The 
Committee was made up of representa¬ 
tives of the Girl Guides: Mrs. Buch- 
bach, Provincial Guide Commissioner: 
Mr. T. Stark, Provincial Scout Com¬ 
missioner; Mr. E. McKenzie, Audio 
Visual Service Branch: Mr. H. Staines 
of the Centennial Office: and myself, 
with a background of YWCA camping, 
church camps and Girl Guides. There 


was opposition to our plan, doubt, and 
such remarks as “it won’t work”, “it 
can’t work”, “it will drag out preju¬ 
dices”, even “it’s impossible”. Somehow 
the more opposition, the stronger grew 
our conviction that we’d make it work. 

We wrote and revised briefs and 
finally had a workable one, which was 
taken to the Centennial Corporation in 
January, requesting $4,000.00. Once 
again there was opposition, and such 
remarks as “do young people want to 
be recognized as from another origin, 
or do they want to identify as Cana¬ 
dians”—to which we replied, “What is 
a Canadian?”. 

Mr. Gardiner, Public Works minister, 
suggested, that because of the need 
amongst Indian and Metis for help and 
recognition and also because as a pilot 
project we had to begin somewhere, 
perhaps we should concentrate this year 
on Indians and Metis. We agreed so 
long as the door was not completely 
closed on other Ethnic people, and we 
had our grant. 

The first step was to contact all the 
established camps in Saskatchewan and 
send a form letter. The amount of 
$30.00 per guest camper was allotted 
and a set of booklets on Indian lore. 
Saskatchewan songs and other informa¬ 
tion was made available. 

The Centennial Corporation gave the 
project some wonderful publicity which 
resulted in requests coming from groups 
of which we were unaware. Motives 


94 


Canadian Camping 



were varied—some genuinely were pro¬ 
moting inter-cultural friendship — to 
some the grant looked good. All requests 
were read, and numbers of the guests 
were allocated in ratio to the full regis¬ 
tration of camp. 

In some instances the location of 
guests posed no problem—missionaries 
made sympathetic and practical con¬ 
tacts. Some Directors found youngsters, 
interviewed, outfitted them and had 
everything in order, but—when they 
went to pick up the children, the entire 
family had vanished into the bush— 
“gone fishing?” — “maybe a buflfalo 
hunt?”—who knows—they just weren’t 
there. 

In my own experience, I had five 
guests ready until ten days before camp 
and on final check couldn’t find them, 
so requested names through the Indian 
Meti Friendship Center, interviewed 
them and their families and as a result 
our own camp was much richer because 
of the presence of five remarkable young 
girls. 

Our guests swam like Otters (much 
the same style too), were naturals in 
canoeing and taught the primary area 
to do Indian dances and some fairly 
creditable chanting. One of the girls 
in the senior area gave a moving por¬ 
trayal of Louis Riel in a play which 
her cabin group wrote and produced. 
Others took part in typical western 
blood and thunder skits with “good 
guys” and “bad guys” sharing the 
honours. 

At the end of each camp, the director 
sent in a list of guests and an evalua¬ 
tion. The evaluations varied in length 


but all had one thing in common—it 
had been a good experience for all 
concerned. 

In one Guide camp, the guests were 
supplied with clothing and sleeping bags 
—even spending money. Two girls 
enjoyed the camp so much they joined 
the Guide company. One evaluation 
said their guests “integrated without a 
ripple”, which could have meant many 
things. 

All indicated that they would like to 
participate again and make this a con¬ 
tinuing project. The guest campers 
parted—some tearfully, most of them 
exchanging addresses and promising to 
write to new found friends. 

Approximately 200 guest campers 
were absorbed into Camps from the far 
northern area of Saskatchewan to the 
southern section and from East to West 
and were represented in most faiths 
and creeds: Anglican Camps; Roman 
Catholic Gamps; United Church 
Camps; Apostolic Camps; Baptist 
Camps; Lutheran Camps; Church ol 
Christ Camps; YWCA Camps; Camp 
Easter Seal for Crippled Children; Girl 
Guides; Boy Scouts; YMCA; Ukrainian 
Youth Association and 4H. 

The $4,000.00 was not enough — an 
additional $2,000.00 was requested, 
received and used. 

We held our first meeting for this 
season last week and are now rolling 
up our sleeves, ready to begin again, 
armed with more knowledge, wary of 
last year’s mistakes and hopeful that 
our venture will be carried on for 
many, many years to come. 

—• 


Jin jfflemortam 

The entire camping fraternity will be saddened to hear of 
the passing of Miss Dais Gass, February 14th. 

One of the original founders of the Canadian Camping Associa¬ 
tion, Director of Camp Memphamagog in Quebec, and active 
in C.G.I.T. work for many years previous to that. Miss Gass 
will be sorely missed by all who knew and loved her.

For Your Reading 

If you read “Hitting the Trail in 
Canada” by Melba Woelfle, which 
appeared in the November 1965 issue 
of Community Recreation (publishedby 
the Community Programmes Branch, 
Department of Education, Victoria, 
B.C.), you will know that in 1964 some 
sixty-one thousand walkers took to the 
nature trails in Ontario’s provincial 
parks—an increase of a thousand per¬ 
cent in a five year period. 

And in another very interesting pam¬ 
phlet, “Hiking Trails in Canada” pub¬ 
lished by the Greb Hiking Bureau, a 
Public Service Organization maintained 
by Greb Shoes Ltd., you can get a con¬ 
siderable amount of information about 
hiking trails available across the entire 
country. It also lists the Canadian 
organizations engaged in hiking. 

WATER FUN FOR EVERYONE 

Developed by members of the 26 
American organizations of the U.S. 
Council for National Co-operation in 
Aquatics, a book has been presented 
that should make any possible kind of 
aquatic programme interesting and 
challenging to any age group in camp. 
Games, stunts, parties, shows, contests, 
synchronized swimming are planned 
and illustrated on paper; instructions 
for leading all of them make the whole 
programme foolproof when directors 
and counsellors read and study the 
procedures. We like the fun approach, 
the emphasis on safety, and the fact 
that the book includes games and 
stunts to make water activities fun for 
the eager beginner. This one should be 
top-of-the-list buying for all of us who 
want waterfront programmes to have 
meaning. G. R. Welch Company, 
Limited, Toronto. $6.50.

FROM 

THE PROVINCES 

Reading the annual reports which 
have come from some of the Provincial 
Associations gives us the impression 
that the upgrading of Leadership and 
Standards is becoming a matter of com¬ 
mon concern, and we look forward to 
hearing more about this development. 

Cooking for Camps caught our eye 
in the B.C. report. With the assistance 
of the Vancouver School Board Night 
Schools, a ten week course was set up 
at a charge of $10.00. Maybe the B.C. 
people would like to “tell us more” in 
“Canadian Camping”. 

Alberta sponsored a Camp Directors’ 
Seminar at Banff where the emphasis 
was on “The Future of Camping” and, 
if we’re to believe the really knowledge¬ 
able ones in this field, it can be quite 
a future. 

In Manitoba, Camp Directors look¬ 
ing for Staff, and Counsellors looking 
for jobs will be glad to hear that the 
Association there is working towards 
the establishment of a central office to 
handle enquiries. 

Ontario met with the Social Plan¬ 
ning Council and the Department of 
Education to pool ideas on leadership 
training. Already their thoughts arc 
winging towards March 2-4, 1967 
when they will host the C.C.A. Cen¬ 
tennial Conference. 

Quebec’s concern for standards re¬ 
sulted in their securing the services of 
Mr. Murray McFarlane who visited 
twenty-seven camps during the summer 
months, and completed an exhaustive 
report on each camp. The camps were 
charged $25.00 for the visit, said visit 
to be made one every three years. 
A detailed report was submitted to the 
Standards Committee, and letters of

CANADA IS CREAT FOR CAMPINC 

(Some thoughts after attending the Annual Canadian Camping Association Meeting) 


There is a big dividend for presidents 
of provincial associations of the Cana¬ 
dian Camping Association if they can 
manage to attend the Annual Board 
Meeting and stay on for a provincial 
conference such as we did this Febru¬ 
ary. It was a long way for some of us 
to travel, but it was worth every hour 
“lost” by the change of time! 

I was looking forward to meeting the 
friends I had made in Banff in 1963, 
and hoping to recapture the feeling of 
camaraderie which pervaded all our 
activities' there. Well, it happened 
again! The camp administrator’s semi¬ 
nar put on by the British Columbia 
Camping Association was excellent. 
Here is a wonderful group of keen, 
progressive camp people, eager to learn 
and willing to share. Geographically, 
there are so many differences between 
provinces that every conceivable type 
of out-of-doors experience is available 
to our Canadian youth. And it is very 
stimulating to hear about exciting new 
ideas which might be adapted to condi¬ 
tions back home. 

Many aspects of modern day camp¬ 
ing were daily routine for our fore- 

From the Provinces 
from page 97 

accreditation were then forwarded to 
twenty-five camps which pased. Notices 
went to the two who did not meet the 
standards. 

Nova Scotia, too, had a Camp Direc¬ 
tors’ Seminar and Camp Leadership 
Course—an annual project. It was held 
in the spring for five days at a camp 
site and the special lecturer was Dr. 
Hcdley G. Dimock, Director of the 
Centre for Human Relations and Com¬ 
munity Studies, Sir George Williams 
University, Montreal, P.Q. 

All the Associations are participating 


fathers, who opened up our country. 
They were daring and courageous 
people with vision and determination. 
The farther west they went the tougher 
they had to be. Anyone with imagina¬ 
tion and some sensitivity, flying over the 
plains, the mountains and the deep 
valleys can relive the struggles they had 
with the terrain and the elements. 

Now the jet age makes it readily 
possible to come together.to exchange 
ideas and to discuss the many different 
and exciting ways of achieving our 
common goals. I am sure I share the 
feeling of everyone who attended the 
seminar in Vancouver that camping is 
on the move. It doesn’t matter how 
long ago a camp was founded. It is the 
present and the future that counts. 

I believe that our Centenary Journey 
can be the greatest thing that has ever 
happened for camping in Canada. The 
co-operative planning is already cross¬ 
ing provincial boundaries. Participation 
in this project will inspire our youth to 
encompass the whole of our country 
when they say. Canada! 

—Adclc Ebbs 


in Centennial Journeys but about that

To conclude, may' we remind you 
that “Canadian Camping” is the offi¬ 
cial publication of the Canadian Camp¬ 
ing Association and as such is eager to 
serve all the Associations across the 
countiy. So, will you help us to do 
our job by sending in to the Editor, 
snippets, of news, special projects, what 
people are doing in the camping field 
in your province. In that way we’ll be 
able to keep in touch with each other 
and be truly' a national association.

Canadian Camping 



society or sooones 

by W. Fayter, Principal 
Cherook Park Elementary School 
Calgary, Alta. 


It just burns me up when I ‘sec 
people around me wanting to sec things 
done but who aren’t willing or pre¬ 
pared to tackle it themselves, and . „ . 
oh! yes! . . . when I hear people say 
. . . “But this is a recreational organs 
ization. we shouldn’t have to do that” 
or “You know we’re a part of the rec¬ 
reational movement and that shouldn’t 
be expected of us” . . . Garbage, I say 
. . . As one noted scholar says, “It’s 
about time we took the ear plugs out 
and got off* our comfortable cushions”. 
Sure . . . we all realize that conformity 
is sweeping the country and while more 
and more people want to get seats in 
the grandstand, fewer and fewer want 
to sweat it out down on the field. More 
and more people who go out looking 
for jobs are asking: “What can you do 
for me?” rather than “What can I do 
for you?” They want to discuss the 
extras they’re going to get. They want 
to know how cool it’s going to be in 
summer and how warm in winter and 
how safe at all times of the year. The 
progress may be slow and the. glory 
may be small, but the work is steady. 
It just seems to me that this non¬ 
involvement has become an accepted 
way of life. 

I want to refer to a six-letter word 
which was recently referred to me and 
that word is square. “SQUARE”— 
maybe this is where we belong—let’s 
find out. First of all, it wasn’t too 
many years ago that the word “square” 
was one of the finest words in our 
language—you gave a man a square 
deal if you were honest—and you gave 
him a square meal when he was hungry 
—when you got out of debt you were 


square with the world—and that was 
when you could look at your fellow 
man square in the eye—well, so much 
for that. Then some strange characters 
got hold of this word, bent it all inside 
out and gave it back to us, and here 
it is — now everyone knows what a 
square is — he’s the one who never 
learned to get away with it—a fool 
who. volunteers when he doesn’t have 
to—a boob who gets so lost in his work 
that he has to be reminded to go home 
—a slob who still gets all choked up 
when the band plays “O! Canada”. 
He doesn’t want to fly now and pay 
later—he doesn’t believe in opening all 
his packages before Christmas. He’s 
burdened down with old fashioned 
ideas of honesty, loyalty, courage and 
thrift, and he may already be on his way 
to extinction. Laughter today is stored 
in cans down in Hollywood just as U.S. 
gold was once stored in Fort Knox. 
It is taken out as needed and pasted 
onto TV films and the laugh track tips 
us off when things are funny. But some 
people want to laugh when amused and 
some want to decide for themselves 
what they think is funny. This might 
well mark them as squares—but, if it 
docs, they will be in pretty good com¬ 
pany. For this country was discovered, 
put together, fought over and saved by 
squares. 

It is easy to prove that Champlain, 
Brock, Graham, Bell, Bishop, Dr. Bant¬ 
ing and almost anyone else you care 
to include among our national heroes 
were squares—by simply thinking of 
the attitudes they might have taken 
had they not been squares. Champlain 
might well have remained at home 


Toronto, Canada, April 1966 


99 



rather than risk his life attempting to 
learn more about the “New World” 
What was he — some kind of nut?” 
Brock could easily have argued he had 
too few men to oppose invading forces 
in the War of 1812, but he didn’t, and 
won anyway. Bell didn't have to work 
night and day to perfect the telephone 
—no one knew then how vital a part 
of our life it was destined to be. Billy 
Bishop should probably have stayed 
away from those flimsy World War I 
airplanes—it would have been much 
safer, wouldn’t it? 

But the greatest thing that has hap¬ 
pened, of course, is that nations have a 
whole new set of heroes named, Glenn, 
Shepherd, Cooper—and these people 
apparently grew up to be squares— 
for who but a square would volunteer 
his life for )iis country’s* good? Being 
a square means being an individual in 
this nation where the forces of con¬ 
formity arc still ever so strong. Too 
many of us are still sitting it out in¬ 
stead of sweating it out! Too many of 
us haven’t got the intestines to stand 
up straight and dare to be square— 
why? Because the opposite of square 
is round, and being round is much 
simpfer. Responsibilities and problems 
roll off nice and easy, and we can just 
glide down the path without encoun¬ 
tering any bumps—being ever so care¬ 
ful to stay in the middle because isn’t 
that Where the most comfortable ruts 
are? 

Far too many of us know the short 
cuts and too few know or care where 
the path leads to. Too few of us dare 
to leave the path because isn’t the path 
always the easy way?—the way most 


people go. But there is no path to the 
future—no path to greatness—no path 
to outer space or to inner satisfactions. 

Well then, how shall we fight for 
this personal independence? How can 
we avoid this great nothing of cynical 
sophistication and this bored and sick¬ 
ening non-participation. Just think 
about it. 

May I suggest that we all join the 
S.O.S. — the Society of Squares. It 
doesn’t exist, but it wouldn’t take too 
long to organize and we would be for 
participation, and against sitting life 
out—for the honest way, against the 
easy short cut—for a well-done job. 
against the goof-off—for building and 
building, against tearing down. 

Just what is it that I require to have 
the courage to be myself? Let’s give 
this some careful thought—right now— 
Let’s do some down-to-earth, serious 
soul-searching, and put our thoughts 
into action. Let’s take a stand for what 
we think is right, whether it be a 
political or a social issue. Please don’t 
sit in the back row of life and mumble 
away to yourself—out with it. You know 
we haven’t got too long to go and this 
life will be all over for us. Let’s be¬ 
come involved, and then we have all 
the right in the world to criticize—but 
don’t just sit your life away. Just what 
are we doing with the great gift of life 
that has been given to us—Are we 
putting it to good use?—Are we really 
individualists, or are we conformists? 

It’s about time we came to grip with 
life, and the only way that we are 
going to achieve this is through hard 
work and a Spirit of Independence.

registrations — the largest assembly of 
camping people ever held in this 
country. So, il the O.C.A. President, 
Adelc Ebbs, the Conference Chairman, 
Ron Johnstone and all those people 
who worked so hard to make this such 
a brilliant success feel like puffing out 
their chests and strutting a bit, we 
think they’re more than justified in 
doing so!

19th. In every session we were able to 
attend, and certainly in the address to

Random Reflections - continued 
Barry G. Lowes, both overtones and 
undertones put the spotlight on Leader¬ 
ship and Standards. It was a gauntlet 
flung down, a challenge thrown out to 
everyone in the camping field in Can¬ 
ada. “Camping in Canada”, declared 
Mr. Lowes, “is at the crossroads; we 
cannot continue as wc have been doing 
. .. what we do is so much less than what 
wc say we do. What do we give our 
space age children — are our pro¬ 


grammes stimulating enough to attract 
their interest. Wc arc not recognizing 
the individuality of each child nor en¬ 
couraging them to choose—to partici¬ 
pate freely in discussion . . . Camps 
are places where wc can and must give 
a new awareness of God, where spirit¬ 
ual values are caught, not taught . . . 
We can’t stand still; we must make 
good on all our claims or else stand 
aside.” 

Dr. John Rich said a few things we 
remember also—“We’re always com¬ 
paring ourselves with experts—a good 
way to create frustration. Children 
must be taught to find security within 
themselves and set aside their fears of 
being different. We’ve got to stop 
thinking that every discussion has to 
end in understanding and to cease 
thinking we unit have competition in 
every undertaking.” 

There were some excellent exhibits 
and in the evenings pictures to see— 
several movies of camps and campers 
and lively programmes that made one 
want to be there doing just those 
things. 

On Friday night we tripped through 
“the Canadian Barrens” with Mr. and 
Mrs. Eric Morse. What a story they 
told and what pictures they showed of 
journeys in the way out places of Can¬ 
ada—up around the Arctic circle and 
the Yukon and the Mackenzie River 
— travelling by canoe, sleeping in 
tents, shooting the rapids, portaging 
over rugged country, the like of which 
few of us have ever seen. Talk about 
a challenge to youth! 

And, of course, there was the delight 
of meeting old friends and making new 
ones; of small group discussions where 
one could share problems and successes, 
and the excellent, down to earth talk 
about where wc should be going and 
what we should be doing. It was a 
great three days; we can hardly wait 
for March 1967 and the C.C.A. Cen¬ 
tennial Conference. 

—•

England.

contacts with new staff personnel.

publishers of CAMPING MAGAZINE.
